pages.text: Alibaba, a big Chinese company, is suing the U.S. Pentagon. The Pentagon put Alibaba on a list of “Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.” in June 2026. This means Alibaba cannot sell things to the U.S. Department of Defense. Alibaba says it is not connected to the Chinese military. It says the Pentagon’s decision is wrong and stops it from doing business.

Alibaba also says it did not get a chance to explain itself. The U.S. government says Alibaba helps China’s “military-civil fusion” plan. This plan helps move technology from regular companies to the military. The Pentagon says Alibaba is linked to China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Alibaba says it follows all Chinese laws, just like other companies in China.

But the Pentagon says Alibaba also makes technology for censorship, like “Green AI.” This technology helps filter content online. The Pentagon also mentioned that Alibaba had a joint venture with Norinco Group, a military company, to create Qianxun Intelligence. Alibaba sold its share in 2018, but still uses its technology. The Pentagon also points to Alibaba’s partnerships with state-owned companies for data centers and satellite technology.

Alibaba says its main business is for regular people and businesses, not the military. This lawsuit will test how the U.S. government views Chinese tech companies. MIIT (Bộ Công nghiệp và Công nghệ thông tin): Một cơ quan chính phủ Trung Quốc.

pages.text: Alibaba has initiated a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) after being designated a “Chinese military company operating in the U.S.” in June 2026. This classification, part of an expanded Section 1260H list, subjects Alibaba to a Pentagon procurement ban, effectively excluding it from the DoD’s supply chain. The listing also suggests a heightened risk of further sanctions from other U.S. departments.

In its court filing, Alibaba vehemently denied any ties to the Chinese military or involvement in China’s “state-directed military-civil fusion strategy.” The company argues that the listing and ban are “without basis in fact or law” and will significantly harm its future business prospects. Furthermore, Alibaba claims the abrupt announcement violated its constitutional right to present its case. The DoD’s decision is rooted in Section 1260H, introduced in 2021 to counter China’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, which aims to transfer commercial technology to defense bases.

The DoD’s statement describes Alibaba as “indirectly affiliated with SASAC” and a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base” due to its affiliation with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The Pentagon’s evidence, drawn from public records and news reports, highlights Alibaba’s alignment with China’s government strategies, including censorship and technology development. The DoD specifically cites Alibaba’s role in building China’s censorship regime, referencing its “Green AI” technology, which automates real-time content filtering and is sold to various platforms.

Alibaba counters that compliance with Chinese regulations, which all multinational companies must adhere to, should not be misconstrued as evidence of military connections. However, the DoD’s filing also points to Alibaba’s joint venture with Norinco Group, a sanctioned Chinese state-owned military company, in establishing Qianxun Intelligence, which develops spatial intelligence AI using the Beidou Navigation Satellite System. Although Alibaba divested its 50 percent share in Qianxun Intelligence in 2018, its executives reportedly retain significant control, and Alibaba continues to rely on Qianxun AI for commercial products.

The DoD further notes Alibaba’s partnerships with state-owned enterprises like China Mobile for data centers and China National Nuclear Power Co. for electricity supply, as well as its acquisition of a stake in Shanghai Spacecom Satellite Technology to develop the Qianfan Constellation (千帆星座). These collaborations, the DoD argues, demonstrate an indirect affiliation with SASAC and support China’s civil-military fusion strategy. Alibaba maintains that its core business serves commercial and individual consumers, not the military.

Qianfan Constellation (千帆星座): Một chòm sao vệ tinh quỹ đạo thấp tương tự Starlink của SpaceX. SASAC (Ủy ban Giám sát và Quản lý Tài sản Nhà nước): Một cơ quan đặc biệt trực thuộc Quốc vụ viện Cộng hòa Nhân dân Trung Hoa. Norinco Group: Một công ty quân sự nhà nước của Trung Quốc bị Bộ Tài chính Hoa Kỳ trừng phạt.

pages.text: Alibaba has initiated legal proceedings against the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), challenging its inclusion on the Section 1260H list of “Chinese military companies operating in the U.S.” The designation, made in June 2026, subjects Alibaba to a Pentagon procurement ban, effectively severing its access to the DoD’s supply chain and signaling an elevated risk of further sanctions from the Departments of Commerce or the Treasury. In its court filing, Alibaba unequivocally refutes any affiliation with the Chinese military or participation in China’s “state-directed military-civil fusion strategy.” The company asserts that the listing and subsequent ban are “without basis in fact or law,” contending that these actions will significantly curtail its future commercial opportunities.

Furthermore, Alibaba argues that the abrupt nature of the announcement infringed upon its constitutional right to due process and the opportunity to articulate its position. Section 1260H, enacted in 2021, was designed to counter China’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, which aims to facilitate the transfer of commercial technological advancements and research to Chinese defense entities. The DoD’s rationale for listing Alibaba describes it as “indirectly affiliated with SASAC” (State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council of the People’s Republic of China) and a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base,” primarily due to its ties with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT).

The DoD’s evidentiary submission to the court, comprising international and Chinese domestic news reports, underscores the authoritative nature of China’s big-tech governance model. These records, the DoD contends, highlight Alibaba’s strategic alignment with the Chinese government’s objectives in censorship, technology, and military development. Specifically, the DoD cites Alibaba’s active role in constructing China’s censorship infrastructure, referencing its “Green AI” technology, which automates real-time content filtering across various media and is marketed to both domestic and international developers, e-commerce vendors, and streaming platforms to ensure compliance with Chinese legal requirements.

Alibaba counters that its adherence to Chinese regulatory frameworks, a prerequisite for all multinational corporations operating within China, including American firms, should not be misconstrued as evidence of military ties. However, the Pentagon’s public record attachment also details Alibaba’s historical joint venture with Norinco Group, a Chinese state-owned military company sanctioned by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. This collaboration led to the establishment of Qianxun Intelligence, a developer of spatial intelligence AI leveraging the Beidou Navigation Satellite System for precise positioning in various applications.

Although Alibaba divested its 50 percent share in Qianxun Intelligence in 2018, it is alleged that its executive members retain substantial control, and Alibaba continues to integrate Qianxun AI into its commercial product offerings. Further substantiating its claims, the DoD points to Alibaba’s partnerships with state-owned enterprises such as China Mobile for cloud computing and AI data centers, and its recent joint venture with China National Nuclear Power Co. in Ningbo to secure stable electricity for future data centers. Additionally, Alibaba’s acquisition of a stake in Shanghai Spacecom Satellite Technology to develop the Qianfan Constellation (千帆星座), a low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation, is cited.

The DoD argues that these extensive collaborations with state-owned entities, particularly in strategic sectors like data centers and geospatial technology, demonstrate an indirect affiliation with SASAC and contribute to China’s civil-military fusion strategy. Alibaba, a private company dual-listed in the U.S. and Hong Kong, maintains that its core business operations, encompassing cloud services, e-commerce, and logistics, are exclusively geared towards commercial enterprises and individual consumers, not the military sector. Qiushi (求是): Một tạp chí lý luận chính trị của Đảng Cộng sản Trung Quốc. Beidou Navigation Satellite System: Hệ thống định vị vệ tinh của Trung Quốc. Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC): Cơ quan quản lý không gian mạng của Trung Quốc.

We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet." This extreme weather is due to El Niño, a natural event that causes very hot or dry weather in Latin America.

This makes it hard for farmers to grow food. El Niño makes food security worse. Food security means that people have enough food to eat. In 2025, about 2.1 billion people did not have enough good food. Lena Savelli from the World Food Programme (WFP) says that El Niño will make crops like corn and rice grow less.

This will make food more expensive, especially for families with low incomes. Latin America exports food, but it costs almost five dollars per person per day for a healthy diet there. Many people cannot afford this. Experts say El Niño will get stronger. Small farmers provide 80 percent of the food in Latin America.

When they lose crops, it is a big problem. Christian Domínguez, a researcher, says that El Niño has always happened, but climate change is making it worse. Areas like Central America and the Caribbean will have droughts, while Ecuador and Peru might have floods. Governments need to help people adapt and prevent problems. Early warning systems can tell farmers when to plant.

Climate insurance can also help people who lose money because of bad weather. El Niño also affects health, jobs, and transport. Informal workers are most at risk. New maps show changes in the ocean that affect marine life. We need to learn to live with these changes and use early warning systems to respond.

pages.text: René Luna, a farmer in central Bolivia, describes his despair after a heavy snowfall, which buried hundreds of his animals, including llamas, alpacas, and sheep. He stated, "We are sad, completely desperate. We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet." This region has been declared a disaster zone. This extreme weather event is linked to El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate phenomenon that causes severe temperatures or insufficient rainfall in Latin America, leading to significant crop losses for rural communities.

The livelihoods of many Latin American families depend on agriculture, but this system is increasingly vulnerable to climate-related disruptions. The 2026 “State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World” report revealed that 25.8 percent of the global population, approximately 2.1 billion people, faced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025. This meant they often had to choose less nutritious or smaller quantities of food. Despite a slight decline in hunger globally, improvements remain fragile and uneven.

Lena Savelli, Regional Director of the World Food Programme (WFP), explains that food security is influenced by conditions in the fields, market prices and availability, and families' purchasing power. She predicts that "droughts or extreme rainfall […] will reduce the yields of key crops such as corn, beans, rice, and even cocoa and coffee, which will see their supply shrink and prices rise in markets and stores." This will make food more expensive and less varied, particularly for low-income households.

Latin America, despite being a major food exporter, has the highest cost for a healthy diet globally, at almost five dollars per person per day, making it unaffordable for millions. El Niño is expected to intensify, with several countries already declaring emergencies. Jhenifer Mojica, an agricultural expert, highlights that smallholder family farming, including Indigenous communities, forms the backbone of food supply, accounting for 80 percent of food security in Latin America.

She warns of "an enormous amount of losses," citing forest fires in Tolima, a key agricultural region in Colombia. Christian Domínguez of UNAM notes that while El Niño is natural, climate change is intensifying its effects, leading to more severe droughts, heavy rains, and heat waves. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) identifies the Central American Dry Corridor, the Caribbean, and northern South America as high-risk areas for droughts and water shortages. Conversely, Ecuador and Peru's Pacific coasts may experience extreme rainfall and flooding.

While governments are responding to emergencies, effective prevention requires addressing structural issues like inequality and weak social mobility. Strengthening local food systems and implementing early warning systems, as seen in Central America’s Dry Corridor, are crucial. Climate insurance also offers protection against economic losses from extreme weather. The International Labour Organization (ILO) report, "El Niño 2026-2027 and the World of Work in Latin America and the Caribbean," emphasizes that informal, rural, and outdoor workers are most exposed, viewing El Niño as a significant test of the region's institutional resilience.

pages.text: René Luna, a farmer in a central Bolivian municipality now designated a disaster zone, recounts the devastating impact of an unprecedented heavy snowfall. He lamented, "We are sad, completely desperate. We have lost llamas, alpacas, sheep — we haven’t even been able to count them all yet." This catastrophic event, which buried hundreds of his livestock, underscores the escalating vulnerability of agricultural communities to extreme weather phenomena. Experts attribute this situation to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate pattern characterized by anomalous warming of equatorial Pacific surface waters, which in Latin America manifests as extreme temperatures or a pronounced lack of rainfall during the wet season, leading to widespread crop failures and the decimation of livelihoods.

The intricate chain of food security in Latin America, encompassing agricultural production, distribution networks, and consumer access, is increasingly compromised by climate-related disruptions. The 2026 edition of the “State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World” report, compiled by five international organizations, revealed that 25.8 percent of the global populace, approximately 2.1 billion individuals, experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025. This necessitated compromises on food quality or quantity. Paradoxically, while global hunger showed a third consecutive year of decline, these improvements are acknowledged as fragile and uneven, highlighting persistent systemic challenges. Lena Savelli, Regional Director of the World Food Programme (WFP), delineates three critical factors influencing food security in the context of ENSO: agricultural field conditions, market dynamics of prices and availability, and household purchasing power and dietary patterns.

She forecasts that "droughts or extreme rainfall […] will reduce the yields of key crops such as corn, beans, rice, and even cocoa and coffee, which will see their supply shrink and prices rise in markets and stores." This anticipated reduction in supply and concomitant price inflation will disproportionately affect low-income families, exacerbating food insecurity. Despite Latin America and the Caribbean's status as a net food-exporting region, it paradoxically bears the highest global cost for a healthy diet, averaging almost five dollars per person per day, rendering it unaffordable for millions and contributing to a dual burden of hunger and obesity. The WFP's monitoring indicates an expected intensification of El Niño during the latter half of the year, with several countries already declaring emergencies.

Jhenifer Mojica, an agricultural expert and former Colombian ambassador to the FAO, emphasizes the foundational role of smallholder family farming, including Indigenous peoples and local communities, in regional food supply, asserting that 80 percent of Latin American food security relies on these producers. She warns of "an enormous amount of losses," citing recent forest fires in Tolima, a predominantly agricultural region in Colombia, as an example where a harvest loss represents the depletion of a farming family’s entire assets. Christian Domínguez, a researcher at UNAM’s Institute of Atmospheric Sciences and Climate Change, clarifies that while ENSO is a natural climate variability, anthropogenic climate change is amplifying its intensity, leading to more severe droughts, heavy rains, and heat waves.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has identified the Central American Dry Corridor, the Caribbean, and northern South America as regions at heightened climate risk, particularly susceptible to droughts, water shortages, and heat waves. Conversely, Ecuador’s and Peru’s Pacific coasts are projected to face extreme rainfall and flooding, while southeastern South America is expected to experience above-average precipitation and severe storms. While governmental responses to immediate emergencies are evident, a substantial gap remains in effective preventative strategies. Savelli advocates for addressing structural determinants, including persistent inequality, weak social mobility, and inadequate diets, and strengthening local food systems to ensure market access for agricultural produce. Promising initiatives, such as early warning systems paired with practical prevention messaging and climate insurance, have emerged in areas like Central America’s Dry Corridor, offering mechanisms to mitigate economic losses from extreme weather.

The ramifications of El Niño extend beyond agriculture, impacting access to basic services, public health (due to increased mosquito populations), infrastructure, transportation, and employment. The International Labour Organization (ILO) report, “El Niño 2026-2027 and the World of Work in Latin America and the Caribbean,” highlights the particular vulnerability of informal, rural, and outdoor workers. The report concludes that "El Niño 2026-2027 is, above all, a test of Latin America’s institutional resilience at a moment when external shocks keep piling up." Satellite imagery already reveals visible effects, with new maps showing significantly lower chlorophyll concentrations in the equatorial Pacific, signaling disruptions to the marine food web. Domínguez reiterates the imperative for adaptation and the implementation of robust early-warning systems to navigate the intensified climate phenomena.
